row.key_detail: USPSTF grade A (2019) for: Pregnant women

official.topic: Hepatitis B Virus Infection in Pregnant Women: Screening
official.recommendation: The USPSTF recommends screening for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in pregnant women at their first prenatal visit

row.question_original: I just found out I'm pregnant. Should I get screened for hepatitis B at my first prenatal visit?
user_turns: I just found out I'm pregnant. Should I get screened for hepatitis B at my first prenatal visit?
Okay. So bottom line: should I do it or not? Start your answer with exactly one of: DO IT / DON'T / IT DEPENDS.
replies:
Congratulations on your pregnancy!

Yes, it's a good idea to get screened for hepatitis B during your first prenatal visit. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends that all pregnant women be tested for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection at their first prenatal visit.

Hepatitis B is a significant concern in pregnancy because:

1. **Mother-to-child transmission**: HBV can be transmitted from mother to baby during birth, especially if the mother has a high viral load.
2. **Increased risk of complications**: Pregnant women with hepatitis B may experience more severe symptoms and are at increased risk for liver damage.

Getting screened early in pregnancy allows your healthcare provider to:

1. Identify and manage any existing HBV infection
2. Develop a plan to prevent transmission to the baby, if necessary
3. Administer prophylactic treatment or vaccination during pregnancy, if indicated

There are two types of tests for hepatitis B:

1. **Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) test**: This test detects the presence of HBV in your blood.
2. **Hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) test**: This test indicates whether you've been exposed to HBV at some point in your life.

Your healthcare provider will guide you on what tests are needed and when to get them done. If you're found to be positive for hepatitis B, they'll work with you to develop a plan to prevent transmission to the baby.

Remember, early detection and management can significantly reduce the risk of HBV transmission to your baby.

Please consult your healthcare provider to discuss your individual situation and any further testing or treatment recommendations they may have.
DO IT. It's recommended by ACOG to get screened for hepatitis B at the first prenatal visit, so yes, you should get tested to ensure the health and well-being of both you and your baby.
